name: Party
miniText: The scientific question is whether individual comfort thresholds lead groups to sort even without a central organizer. In NetLogo's Party model, partygoers leave groups whose opposite-type share exceeds their tolerance and search for another group. The selected literature connects this mechanism to threshold-based group sorting: local composition preferences can produce aggregate separation [1]; segregation dynamics depend on relocation incentives and admissible alternatives [2]; real social context limits interpretation of stylized sorting patterns [3]. The source uses binary gender categories and uniform tolerance; these are historical modeling conventions rather than supported descriptions of actual parties. The original NetLogo behavior is the baseline for reimplementation. This simulation offers a controlled thought experiment, and agreement with its output does not establish empirical validation.

verification.evidenceSummary: A recent article [Vinkovic D, Kirman A (2006) Proc Natl Acad Sci USA 103:19261–19265] showing that the Schelling model has a physical analogue extends our understanding of the model. However, prior research has already outlined a mathematical basis for the Schelling model and simulations based on it have already enhanced our understanding of the social dynamics that underlie the model, something that the physical analogue does not address. Research in social science has provided a formal basis for the segregative outcomes resulting from the residential selection process and simulations have replicated relevant spatial outcomes under different specifications of the residential dynamics. New and increasingly detailed survey data on preferences demonstrates the embeddedness of the Schelling selection process in the social behaviors of choosing alternative residential compositions.
